blocks.text: A cylinder-head stud that is tightened by feel can end up carrying anything from half to nearly all of its proof load, and the engine will either leak gas or shear the stud. The only thing the fitter controls is a torque reading, so engineers must know how a twist on the nut becomes a clamping force in the bolt.

blocks.markdown: A bolt is a spring that is stretched when the nut is tightened. The stretch produces a tensile **preload** $F_i$ in the bolt and an equal compressive **clamp load** on the joint members. Preload is what holds a joint together, resists slip, seals gaskets and, as the last section of this unit shows, protects the bolt from fatigue. Because nobody can put a force gauge inside a joint during assembly, we usually tighten to a torque and infer the preload from it.

blocks.title: Preload and proof load
blocks.text: Preload $F_i$ is the initial tensile force in the bolt after tightening (N). Proof load $F_p=S_pA_t$ is the largest tensile force the bolt can carry without permanent set, where $S_p$ is the proof strength (MPa) and $A_t$ is the tensile stress area (mm$^2$). Proof strength is about 85 to 95 per cent of the yield strength for common grades.

blocks.markdown: **Tensile stress area.** A thread is not a plain cylinder, so the stress in a loaded bolt is referred to an effective area $A_t$ that lies between the pitch-diameter area and the minor-diameter area. For ISO metric threads with nominal diameter $d$ and pitch $p$ (both in mm), the pitch diameter is $d_2=d-0.649519\,p$ and the minor diameter is $d_3=d-1.226869\,p$, and the stress area is the area of a circle of the mean of these two diameters.

blocks.caption: ISO metric tensile stress area (mm^2 when d and p are in mm)

blocks.markdown: **Torque to preload.** Tightening torque $T$ does work against two friction sources, thread friction (and the thread-ramp lift) and friction under the nut face, so only a small share of the effort ends up as bolt tension. Rather than evaluate the thread mechanics every time, designers lump all of it into the dimensionless **torque coefficient** (nut factor) $K$. The value of $K$ is set by friction, not by geometry. Typical values for steel fasteners are about 0.2 for plain dry black bolts, about 0.18 for zinc-plated bolts and about 0.15 for lubricated bolts (these are representative figures, always confirm for the actual finish and lubricant). Because friction scatters, a torque wrench commonly gives preload only to within about $\pm 25$ per cent. **Warning:** Torque and preload are linked only through $K$. If a fitter oils a bolt that the drawing specified dry, the same torque gives a much higher preload, and the bolt may be tightened beyond proof load and stretched permanently. Torque values are always quoted together with a thread condition.

blocks.caption: Short-form torque-tension relation (Shigley convention); T in N m, F_i in N, d in m

blocks.title: Torque for a reusable M12 joint
blocks.prompt: An M12 x 1.75 coarse-thread bolt of property class 8.8 (typical proof strength $S_p=600$ MPa) is to be tightened to the usual reusable-joint preload of $0.75F_p$. Use $K=0.2$. Find the tightening torque.

steps.text: Tensile stress area from the thread geometry. Here $d_2=10.863$ mm and $d_3=9.853$ mm, so the mean diameter is 10.358 mm.
Proof load, remembering that MPa times mm$^2$ gives N.
Target preload at 75 per cent of proof load.
Torque from the torque coefficient, using $d=0.012$ m.

blocks.answer: $A_t\approx 84.3$ mm$^2$, $F_p\approx 50.6$ kN, $F_i\approx 37.9$ kN and the tightening torque is about 91 N m.

Very high strength, fatigue-critical, socket-head screws

blocks.markdown: **Choosing the target preload.** Higher preload gives better clamping and fatigue behaviour, but the bolt must still keep a margin from yielding when the torque twist adds shear stress. A common rule is $F_i\approx 0.75F_p$ for joints that will be taken apart and reassembled, and $F_i\approx 0.90F_p$ for permanent joints, where an over-tightened bolt is not reused. These are design conventions, and the bolt is checked against $F_p$ after external loading is added.

blocks.title: Reading preload back from a wrench
blocks.prompt: A lubricated M16 x 2 bolt of class 8.8 ($S_p=600$ MPa, $A_t=156.7$ mm$^2$) is tightened with a torque wrench to 180 N m. Taking $K=0.15$ for the lubricant, find the preload and compare it with the proof load.

steps.text: Rearrange the torque relation for preload, with $d=0.016$ m.

Compare. The ratio is $75.0/94.0=0.80$, so the bolt is loaded to 80 per cent of proof load. That is above the 75 per cent reusable guideline but below proof, so it is acceptable only if the joint is treated as permanent.

blocks.answer: $F_i=75.0$ kN, which is 80 per cent of the proof load $F_p=94.0$ kN.

blocks.markdown: **Why high preload helps fatigue.** A joint with an external fluctuating load $P$ shares that load between the bolt and the clamped members in proportion to their stiffnesses: the bolt carries the fraction $C=k_b/(k_b+k_m)$ (the joint constant, treated in the next unit) and the members carry the remainder. In a well-preloaded joint the members remain compressed, so the bolt sees only a small alternating force $CP/2$ even when $P$ is large. Without preload, or if the clamp is lost, the bolt would see the whole alternating load.

blocks.caption: Alternating and mean bolt stress for a load P cycling between 0 and P (C is the joint constant, a number below 1)

blocks.title: High preload is protection, not just tightness
blocks.text: Raising $F_i$ raises the bolt mean stress but not its alternating stress, as long as the clamped members stay in compression. Because the fatigue strength of a bolt falls only slowly with mean stress compared with the large reduction in alternating stress, a highly preloaded joint lasts far longer than a loosely tightened one. Preload also prevents separation, fretting at the faces and self-loosening.

points: The torque coefficient $K$ links torque and preload: $T=KF_id$, with $K\approx0.2$ dry and lower when lubricated.
$A_t$ comes from the mean of the pitch and minor diameters, and the proof load is $F_p=S_pA_t$.
Typical target preloads are $0.75F_p$ for reusable and $0.90F_p$ for permanent joints.
High preload keeps the members clamped, so the bolt sees only a fraction $C$ of the external fluctuating load, which greatly improves fatigue life.

questions.stem: In the relation $T=KF_id$ for a tightened bolt, what does the torque coefficient $K$ chiefly represent?

options.text: The friction in the threads and under the nut face, lumped into one dimensionless number
The ratio of the bolt stiffness to the member stiffness
The ratio of the proof strength to the yield strength
The ratio of the stress area to the nominal bolt area

questions.correctOptionText: The friction in the threads and under the nut face, lumped into one dimensionless number

distractorRationale.a: Correct: K absorbs the thread and collar friction (and the thread-lead geometry).
distractorRationale.b: That ratio is the joint constant C, which governs load sharing, not tightening.
distractorRationale.c: Proof strength and yield strength are material properties and do not enter the torque relation.
distractorRationale.d: The stress area ratio affects stress, not how torque converts to preload.

questions.explanation: The torque applied by the wrench is almost entirely spent overcoming friction, with only a small fraction becoming bolt tension. The coefficient $K$ summarises all of that friction, which is why it changes with plating and lubricant.

questions.stem: A bolt specified to be tightened dry to 100 N m is instead assembled with a heavy oil film on the threads and nut face, and the same 100 N m is applied. What happens to the preload?

options.text: It rises, because K falls and a larger share of the torque becomes bolt tension
It falls, because the oil reduces the clamping force
It is unchanged, because the same torque is applied
It falls, because the oil increases the thread friction

questions.correctOptionText: It rises, because K falls and a larger share of the torque becomes bolt tension

distractorRationale.a: Correct: F_i = T/(Kd), so a smaller K gives a larger F_i.
distractorRationale.b: Lower friction releases more of the torque into bolt stretch, so preload rises.
distractorRationale.c: Torque is not the same as preload; the conversion depends on K.
distractorRationale.d: Oil lowers the friction; it does not increase it.

questions.explanation: From $F_i=T/(Kd)$ a lower torque coefficient gives a higher preload for the same torque. This is why lubricated bolts can be tightened beyond proof load if the dry torque value is used.

questions.stem: Why is the tensile stress area $A_t$ of a metric bolt smaller than the area $\pi d^2/4$ based on the nominal diameter?

options.text: The threads remove material, so the effective load-carrying section lies between the pitch-diameter and minor-diameter circles
The steel in the thread is weaker than the steel in the shank
The nominal diameter is measured to the root of the thread
The area is reduced to allow for the safety factor

questions.correctOptionText: The threads remove material, so the effective load-carrying section lies between the pitch-diameter and minor-diameter circles

distractorRationale.a: Correct: A_t is based on the mean of the pitch and minor diameters.
distractorRationale.b: Material strength is the same; it is the section that is reduced.
distractorRationale.c: The nominal diameter is the major (crest) diameter, not the root.
distractorRationale.d: A_t is a geometric area; no safety factor is built into it.

questions.explanation: The cut thread form reduces the section carrying tension, so the effective area is taken from a diameter that is the mean of the pitch and minor diameters. For an M12 x 1.75 bolt this gives about 84 mm$^2$ against 113 mm$^2$ for the nominal circle.

questions.stem: An M10 x 1.5 class 8.8 bolt ($S_p=600$ MPa, $A_t=58.0$ mm$^2$) is tightened to 55 N m with $K=0.2$. What fraction of its proof load is the preload?

options.text: About 79 %
About 58 %
About 158 %
About 40 %

distractorRationale.a: Correct: F_i = 55/(0.2 x 0.010) = 27.5 kN and F_p = 34.8 kN, so the ratio is 0.79.
distractorRationale.b: 58 % results from using the nominal area pi d^2/4 = 78.5 mm^2 instead of A_t for the proof load.
distractorRationale.c: 158 % results from using K = 0.1 instead of 0.2.
distractorRationale.d: 40 % results from using K = 0.4 instead of 0.2.

questions.explanation: The preload is $F_i=T/(Kd)=55/(0.2\times0.010)=27.5$ kN, and the proof load is $F_p=600\times58.0=34.8$ kN. The ratio is therefore 0.79, slightly above the 0.75 guideline for reused joints.

questions.stem: Two identical joints carry the same fluctuating external load. Joint A is tightened to a high preload and joint B is only finger-tight. Which statement best explains why joint A has the longer bolt fatigue life?

options.text: In A the members stay clamped, so the bolt carries only a small fraction of the load fluctuation; in B the bolt carries nearly all of it
In A the bolt has a lower mean stress, which always improves fatigue life
In A the preload adds to the external load, so the load fluctuation is smaller
In A the bolt material becomes stronger when it is stretched

questions.correctOptionText: In A the members stay clamped, so the bolt carries only a small fraction of the load fluctuation; in B the bolt carries nearly all of it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: load sharing through the clamped members reduces the alternating stress in the bolt.
distractorRationale.b: The mean stress in A is higher, not lower; the benefit comes from the smaller alternating stress.
distractorRationale.c: The preload does not reduce the load fluctuation; it changes how the fluctuation is shared.
distractorRationale.d: Tightening does not strengthen the material.

questions.explanation: Preloaded members stay in compression and absorb most of the load swing, so the bolt's alternating stress is only $CP/(2A_t)$. A finger-tight joint is free to open, so the bolt takes the whole load cycle and fatigues early.

questions.stem: The thread of an M20 bolt has nominal diameter $d=20$ mm and coarse pitch $p=2.5$ mm. Using $d_2=d-0.649519p$, $d_3=d-1.226869p$ and $A_t=\frac{\pi}{4}\left(\frac{d_2+d_3}{2}\right)^2$, find the tensile stress area in mm$^2$.
questions.explanation: The pitch diameter is $d_2=20-1.6238=18.376$ mm and the minor diameter is $d_3=20-3.0672=16.933$ mm, giving a mean of 17.654 mm. Then $A_t=\pi/4\times17.654^2=244.8$ mm$^2$, which agrees with the tabulated value of about 245 mm$^2$.

questions.stem: An M14 x 2 bolt of class 10.9 (typical $S_p=830$ MPa, $A_t=115.4$ mm$^2$) in a permanent joint is to be tightened to $0.90F_p$ using a torque coefficient $K=0.18$. Find the tightening torque in N m.
questions.explanation: The proof load is $F_p=830\times115.4=95.8$ kN, so the target preload is $0.90\times95.8=86.2$ kN. Then $T=KF_id=0.18\times86204\times0.014=217.2$ N m.

questions.stem: A class 12.9 M20 x 2.5 bolt ($A_t=245$ mm$^2$, typical $S_p=970$ MPa) is tightened to 380 N m with a torque coefficient $K=0.20$. Find the tensile stress in the bolt due to preload alone, in MPa. (Ignore the torsional shear stress from tightening.)
questions.explanation: The preload is $F_i=T/(Kd)=380/(0.20\times0.020)=95.0$ kN. The tensile stress is $\sigma=F_i/A_t=95000/245=388$ MPa, about 40 per cent of the proof strength, so this bolt has a lot of reserve.

questions.stem: Explain, with the help of the equations for alternating and mean stress, why increasing the preload in a bolted joint that carries a fluctuating tensile load improves the bolt's fatigue resistance. State the condition under which the argument holds.
markingGuide: Load sharing: the bolt carries the fraction $C=k_b/(k_b+k_m)$ of the external load $P$, and the members carry the rest.
Alternating bolt stress $\sigma_a=CP/(2A_t)$ does not depend on the preload provided the joint does not separate.
Preload raises the mean stress $F_i/A_t$ but fatigue strength is much less sensitive to mean stress than to alternating stress, so the safety factor improves overall.
Condition: the clamp load must stay positive (no separation) throughout the load cycle; once the members unload, the bolt takes the whole load swing.
Secondary benefits: resists slip, fretting, self-loosening and leakage.
questions.explanation: The argument depends on the members staying in compression so that they share the load. Without that, preload only adds mean stress and gives no benefit.

questions.stem: A maintenance team tightens a critical flange with a click torque wrench set to the value in the manual, but the bolts arrive coated with a rust inhibitor oil that was not mentioned in the manual. Discuss the likely consequences for preload and state how the engineer should choose the target preload and check the bolt in the design.
markingGuide: Preload is $F_i=T/(Kd)$; oil lowers $K$, so the preload is higher than intended for the same torque.
The risk is overstressing the bolt towards proof load or yield, or damaging threads, because friction scatter makes preload uncertain by tens of per cent.
Target preload should be chosen from the proof load: about $0.75F_p$ for reusable and $0.90F_p$ for permanent joints, where $F_p=S_pA_t$.
Check the bolt at the highest likely preload (using the lowest likely $K$) and the clamping at the lowest likely preload.
Torque values must be specified with the thread condition, or tension-based methods used for critical joints.
questions.explanation: Torque is only an indirect measure of preload, so uncertainty in friction translates directly into uncertainty in clamp load. A good design allows for that scatter.
